model: claude-opus-5-5 in a Claude Code session
system: You are a careful experimenter who designs measurements. You can only use the tools you are given, and only a limited number of measurements. Choose each measurement so that it helps to tell the two models apart, and say why. At the end say which model the measurements favour and how sure you are, or say that they do not tell the models apart. Do not say that a model is true because it fits.
task: A block of 2 kg slides on a table and slows down; the launcher of this rig cannot start it faster than 4 m/s. Two models of the drag compete: linear drag, v = v0 exp(-g t), and quadratic drag, v = v0 / (1 + k v0 t), with g and k unknown. Each reading of the speed has a standard uncertainty of 0.1 m/s. Choose at most 8 measurements, with a start speed of at most 4 m/s, that tell the two models apart.

steps.text: Plan: the two models differ most clearly in how the decay depends on the start speed. Linear drag gives the same fractional decay v/v0 at a given time for every v0; quadratic drag decays faster from a high start speed (rate k*v0). So I measure at the highest allowed start speed (4 m/s, largest signal relative to 0.1 m/s noise) and at a low start speed (1 m/s), each at two times, to get the shape in time and the v0 dependence. First 4 measurements: v0=4 at t=1 s and t=3 s, v0=1 at t=1 s and t=3 s.

Results so far: v0=4: 3.36 (t=1), 2.44 (t=3); v0=1: 1.01 (t=1), 0.82 (t=3). From v0=4 alone both models fit (linear g about 0.16-0.17 /s; quadratic k about 0.047-0.053 /(m)). The v0=1 data separate them: linear with g=0.17 predicts 0.84 and 0.60 at t=1 and 3 (measured 1.01, 0.82, about 1.7 and 2.2 sigma off), while quadratic with k=0.05 predicts 0.95 and 0.87 (within 1 sigma). To sharpen this I go to a late time, where the predictions diverge most: at t=8 s, linear (g~0.17) predicts about 1.03 m/s from v0=4 and 0.25 m/s from v0=1, while quadratic (k~0.05) predicts about 1.54 and 0.71 m/s. Differences of 5 sigma or more. Measurements 5 and 6: v0=4 and v0=1 at t=8 s.

Results: v0=4, t=8: 1.70; v0=1, t=8: 0.78. The apparent linear rate ln(v0/v)/t is not constant: for v0=4 it falls from 0.17 (t=1) to 0.16 (t=3) to 0.11 (t=8), and for v0=1 at t=8 it is only 0.03. Linear drag requires one g for all of these; the best common g (about 0.1-0.13) still leaves residuals of 3-5 sigma (chi-square about 40 for 6 points). Quadratic drag with one k of about 0.045 predicts 3.39, 2.60, 1.64 (v0=4) and 0.96, 0.88, 0.74 (v0=1), all within 1.6 sigma (chi-square about 4). Before concluding I test this with two new, independent readings chosen where the models still differ most, using the k and g fitted so far as predictions made in advance: (a) a new start speed v0=2 at t=10 s: quadratic predicts about 1.05 m/s, linear (g 0.1-0.13) predicts 0.55-0.74 m/s; (b) an independent repeat of the most discriminating point, v0=1 at t=8 s: quadratic predicts about 0.74, linear 0.35-0.45. These are measurements 7 and 8, the last allowed.

Conclusion (8 measurements used). Data: v0=4: 3.36 (t=1), 2.44 (t=3), 1.70 (t=8); v0=1: 1.01 (t=1), 0.82 (t=3), 0.78 and 0.67 (t=8, two independent readings); v0=2: 1.27 (t=10). Sigma = 0.1 m/s each.

Linear drag: the rate ln(v0/v)/t that it requires to be one constant g comes out 0.17, 0.16, 0.11 for v0=4, 0.03-0.05 for v0=1 at t=8, and 0.05 for v0=2 at t=10. No single g fits: with g=0.10 the residuals are -2.6, -5.2 and -1 sigma (v0=4), +1.1, +0.8, +3.3, +2.2 sigma (v0=1) and +5.3 sigma (v0=2), chi-square roughly 80 for 7 degrees of freedom; other g values make the v0=4 early points or the slow late points worse. Its pre-registered predictions for the two check points (0.55-0.74 and 0.35-0.45 m/s) missed by 5-7 and 2-3 sigma.

Quadratic drag with one k of about 0.042-0.045 /m describes all 8 readings to within about 2.2 sigma, chi-square roughly 10 for 7 degrees of freedom, which is acceptable. It correctly predicted in advance the qualitative features that separate the models: the decay slows as the block slows, and a slow start speed decays far less in fractional terms than a fast one. Its check-point predictions were 1.05 (measured 1.27, +2.2 sigma) and 0.74 (measured 0.67, -0.7 sigma).

Verdict: the measurements strongly favour quadratic drag over linear drag; the likelihood ratio between the best fits is of order exp((80-10)/2), so I am very confident in that ranking between these two models. This does not show that quadratic drag is the true law: the fit is only adequate, with mild tension (the v0=2, t=10 reading is high and v0=4, t=3 is low, each about 2 sigma; the k values inferred from single points range from 0.03 to 0.06), so a different or mixed drag law (e.g. some linear plus quadratic, or Coulomb friction) could fit as well or better and is not excluded by 8 readings.
